title: Services, CIM and the event log
summary: Query and change Windows services, read hardware and OS facts with CIM (not WMI), filter the event log fast with -FilterHashtable, and write Windows functions test-first with mocked cmdlets.

steps.title: Windows only: services and CIM
body: > **Windows only.** The commands in this module exist on Windows (in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and in PowerShell 7
> on Windows), not on Linux or macOS. The machine in these lessons is Linux, so the hands-on steps write the
> functions **test-first**, with the Windows cmdlets mocked by Pester: the same way a Linux build agent tests
> Windows tooling.
**Services**
```powershell
Get-Service W3SVC, MSSQLSERVER | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType
Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.StartType -eq 'Automatic' -and $_.Status -ne 'Running' }   # what should run but does not
Restart-Service W3SVC -WhatIf
Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled
In PowerShell 7, service objects also have `BinaryPathName`, `UserName` and `Description`, and there is a
`Remove-Service`. Changing services needs an elevated (administrator) session.
**CIM** (the Common Information Model) is how Windows exposes OS and hardware facts: disks, memory, BIOS, patches.
```powershell
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version, LastBootUpTime
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_LogicalDisk -Filter 'DriveType = 3'          # local fixed disks
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_LogicalDisk -ComputerName fs01, fs02          # remote, over WinRM
`Get-WmiObject` is the old way: it exists only in Windows PowerShell 5.1 (it was **removed in PowerShell 7**) and
talks DCOM, which firewalls usually block. Scripts that still use it are a common reason a 5.1 script fails in 7.
`-Filter` uses WQL and is applied on the target machine: like `-Filter` on `Get-ChildItem`, filter left.

steps.prompt: A 2019-era inventory script uses `Get-WmiObject Win32_LogicalDisk -ComputerName $s`. In PowerShell 7 it fails with *The term 'Get-WmiObject' is not recognized*. What is the right fix?
options: Install the WMI module from the Gallery
steps.explain: Same classes, same properties, newer and firewall-friendlier transport (WinRM). `Get-CimInstance` also works in 5.1, so the fixed script runs in both.

steps.title: Get-LowDisk, test-first
prompt: The team's WinOps module keeps one public function per file under `~/src/WinOps/Public/`. Write
**`Get-LowDisk`** in `~/src/WinOps/Public/Get-LowDisk.ps1`. Its behaviour is defined by
- it calls `Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_LogicalDisk` with a filter for **local fixed disks** (`DriveType = 3`),
- it outputs, for each disk below **`-BelowPercent`** (default **15**) free, an object with `Drive` (the `DeviceID`),
`FreeGB` and `PercentFree`, both rounded to one decimal.
Run `Invoke-Pester ~/src/WinOps/tests/Get-LowDisk.Tests.ps1 -Output Detailed` until it is green.

checks.name: the Get-LowDisk tests pass
checks.cmd: pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -c '$r = Invoke-Pester "$env:DOJO_FILES/tests/Get-LowDisk.Tests.ps1" -PassThru -Output None; "$($r.PassedCount) of $($r.TotalCount) pass"; $r.Failed | ForEach-Object { "FAILED: $($_.ExpandedName): $($_.ErrorRecord.Exception.Message)" }'
checks.fail: Not all tests pass yet (the failing ones are listed). The checks run the original test file, so changing your copy does not help.

hints: Build the CIM call as a hashtable and splat it: `$cim = @{ ClassName = 'Win32_LogicalDisk'; Filter = 'DriveType = 3' }`; `if ($ComputerName) { $cim.ComputerName = $ComputerName }`; `Get-CimInstance @cim`.
Build the objects with `ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ Drive = $_.DeviceID; FreeGB = ...; PercentFree = ... } }`, then `Where-Object PercentFree -lt $BelowPercent`.
solution: Lists local fixed disks with less than -BelowPercent free space.
explain: On a real server: `Get-LowDisk -ComputerName (Get-Content servers.txt)` (make `-ComputerName` a `[string[]]`) and
you have a fleet-wide disk report. The stub-and-mock trick in the test file (`function global:Get-CimInstance`
when the command is missing) is how teams run Windows-module tests on cheap Linux CI agents.

steps.title: Windows only: the event log, fast
body: `Get-WinEvent` reads every Windows event log. Filter **at the source** with `-FilterHashtable`: the event log
service then returns only matching events, which is many times faster than reading the whole log and piping it
into `Where-Object`:
```powershell
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'Security'; Id = 4625; StartTime = (Get-Date).AddHours(-24) }
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'System'; ProviderName = 'Service Control Manager'; Level = 2 } -MaxEvents 50
Get-WinEvent -ListLog *PowerShell*          # which logs exist
Event IDs worth knowing: **4624** / **4625** successful / failed logon (Security), **4740** account locked out,
**7036** a service changed state, **1074** a planned shutdown and who asked for it, **6008** and **41** an unexpected
shutdown, **4104** PowerShell script block logging.
The details are in **`.Properties`**, by position (for 4625, index 5 is the target user name and 19 the source IP),
or as XML: `([xml]$e.ToXml()).Event.EventData.Data`. When nothing matches, `Get-WinEvent` writes an error *No
events were found that match the specified selection criteria*, which a report should treat as "zero", not as a
failure. `Get-EventLog` is the old cmdlet: Windows PowerShell 5.1 only, classic logs only.

steps.prompt: Which event ID answers the question?
pairs: Who keeps typing the wrong password?
Who rebooted the server last night?
Did it crash or lose power?

steps.title: Get-FailedLogon, test-first
prompt: Security wants a daily summary of failed logons. Write **`Get-FailedLogon`** in
- one `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable` call for the **Security** log, **event 4625**, since **`-Hours`** ago (default 24);
- output one object per user: `User`, `Count` and `Sources` (the distinct source IPs, sorted), most failures first;
- no matching events is **not** an error: output nothing.

checks.name: the Get-FailedLogon tests pass
checks.cmd: pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -c '$r = Invoke-Pester "$env:DOJO_FILES/tests/Get-FailedLogon.Tests.ps1" -PassThru -Output None; "$($r.PassedCount) of $($r.TotalCount) pass"; $r.Failed | ForEach-Object { "FAILED: $($_.ExpandedName): $($_.ErrorRecord.Exception.Message)" }'
checks.fail: Not all tests pass yet (the failing ones are listed).

hints: `$events = Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'Security'; Id = 4625; StartTime = (Get-Date).AddHours(-$Hours) } -ErrorAction Stop`, inside `try`.
In `catch`: `if ($_.Exception.Message -like 'No events were found*') { return }; throw`.

`$events | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ User = $_.Properties[5].Value; Ip = $_.Properties[19].Value } } | Group-Object User | Sort-Object Count -Descending | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ User = $_.Name; Count = $_.Count; Sources = @($_.Group.Ip | Sort-Object -Unique) } }`
solution: Failed logons (event 4625) per user over the last -Hours, with their source addresses.
explain: Reading the Security log needs admin rights (or membership of *Event Log Readers*). For a domain, the same question
is usually answered by the SIEM that collects these events, but this function is what you run on one box during
an incident, and `-ComputerName` makes it work remotely.

steps.prompt: Put the query together: the newest 20 errors from the System log in the last 6 hours, shown oldest first, as a table.
steps.explain: Level 2 is *Error* (1 Critical, 3 Warning, 4 Information). `Get-WinEvent` returns newest first, so `-MaxEvents 20` gives the newest 20; sort them for reading, and `Format-Table` last, for eyes only.
